title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England
description: ByHayley Clarke and Beth RoseEducation reportersThere will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the go
body: ByHayley Clarke and Beth RoseEducation reportersThere will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade.Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored.The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers".The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said.As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools. They also must now be served with a portion of fruit.Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country".The Department for Education said it hoped the reforms would tackle childhood obesity, improve nutrition and support children's concentration, learning and wellbeing.Schools will be required to publish food policies and menus online with monitoring arrangements set to be developed alongside the Food Standards Agency, it said. Pepe Di'Iasio, ASCL general secretary, said parents would feel "reassured" that schools were providing children with a healthy diet.But on plans for enforcement, he added: "None of us would consider ourselves experts in health and nutrition. Don't create another stick with which to beat head teachers when they are trying to do their very best to provide a healthy, balanced meal for those in our schools."He said schools needed "more investment" in catering facilities and in the "professional development" of school chefs to develop menus that "meet the ambitions" of the government.As part of the changes, deep-fried chips will have to be oven-baked instead, and pasta dishes will need to be 50% wholewheat once a week. High-fibre bread will also become a requirement. Image caption, Under the new rules, all dishes must come with at least one portion of fruit or vegetablesBreakfast clubs will undergo one of the biggest changes.Historically, there has been no guidance on what they should provide, but from next September pastries and fried-eggs will be off the menu and there will be a sugar cap when it comes to cereals.The government said Coco Pops would no longer be an option and chocolate spread was "not permitted".Since February this year, 1,250 schools have offered free breakfast clubs to their pupils. One of those was Oasis Blakenhale in Birmingham, where principal Farzana Ahmed said the school welcomed the changes."The more children that can access a hot, nutritious meal, the better it is for us, the better it is for them, and actually it really supports families with the reduction of their financial pressures at home," she said.Ahmed said it was "important" that schools are monitored, but added that they "probably need some more guidance from the government on what that's going to look like on a day-to-day basis".Image caption, Farzana Ahmed welcomed both the new school food standards and the expansion of free school meals eligibilityAbout 60% of pupils at the inner-city school receive free school meals, and Ahmed said they were already providing a healthy, balanced diet.With free school meal eligibility expanding this year to all families who receive Universal Credit, Ahmed said there had been an "influx of parents" applying, and expects around 70% of pupils to benefit going forward."It's a really positive move," she said."We know how important a nutritional diet is to the wellbeing, to the behaviour, to the learning of our pupils."Working mum-of-three Kinza Butt said the free school meals her son was now getting at Blakenhale Juniors had lifted a "burden off the shoulders"."He doesn't have to eat those cold sandwiches anymore," she said."By the end of the day he used to be starving. But now he's coming home all happy because he's having good, healthy meals with a snack as well."Image caption, Newly-eligible parent Kinza is delighted her children can now have free school dinnersThe new food standards will apply to primary and secondary schools in England, but rules for school dinners vary across the UK.In Wales, new guidance will come into force by the end of the year with a greater focus on at least two portions of vegetables being offered every day, with only water, milk or plant-based drinks allowed for hydration.Scotland updated its legislation in 2020. It requires students to be offered at least two portions of vegetables and one portion of fruit every day and oily fish must be served at least once every three weeks.Northern Ireland last updated its regulations in 2007. They include providing bread everyday, without spread, and offering two portions of fruit and vegetables a day. It also stipulates that if beans or pulses form the protein part of a main course, another vegetable must be available.

schema.headline: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

title: Gloomy forecast for tenants as rent rises set to speed up
description: It said that rent rises were being seen across the UK, but the situation still differed depending where renters were looking."In less expensive areas,
body: It said that rent rises were being seen across the UK, but the situation still differed depending where renters were looking."In less expensive areas, renters have more capacity to absorb rent rises before hitting an affordability ceiling, whereas in the most expensive areas, rents are already stretching what renters can pay, capping how much further rents can increase," the report said.It predicted a further acceleration in rent rises to 4% or 5% by the end of the year, although that still roughly matched the average annual rise in workers' earnings. New investment in homes to rent by landlords was "still muted as a result of higher costs and more regulation", Zoopla said.Nathan Emerson, chief executive at Propertymark, which represents lettings agents, said the report underlined the need for more high-quality rental homes."A sustainable private rented sector requires the right conditions for responsible landlords to invest for the long term," he said."Increasing supply must remain a priority if we are to give tenants greater choice, improve affordability and create a more stable rental market."

schema.headline: Gloomy forecast for tenants as rent rises set to speed up

title: US Open 2026 results: Alexander Zverev beats Ben Shelton for second Grand Slam title
description: Alexander Zverev used his greater experience to beat home hope Ben Shelton in the US Open final and quiet a partisan crowd hoping to laud a rare Ameri
body: Alexander Zverev used his greater experience to beat home hope Ben Shelton in the US Open final and quiet a partisan crowd hoping to laud a rare American men's champion.German top seed Zverev lifted a heavy burden by winning his first major title at this year's French Open and has quickly added another with a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory over Shelton in New York.At the start of the season, there were question marks over whether 29-year-old Zverev would ever win one of the sport's most prestigious prizes.Now he is celebrating becoming a multiple Grand Slam singles champion, having seen the path to glory partially cleared by injuries to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.Sinner and Alcaraz swept the board between them at the majors in 2024 and 2025 - and Zverev has taken full advantage against the rest of the field in their absences.Big-hitting Shelton, 23, has long been identified as a player who can win the biggest titles, but ultimately came up short in his first Grand Slam final against a rejuvenated Zverev.Eighth seed Shelton was aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick in 2003, but losing serve in the first game of the match set the tone as Zverev controlled the opening two sets.The momentum shifted in the third set, however, as Shelton finally started applying serious pressure on Zverev's serve.Taking his third break opportunity provided encouragement to the 24,000 home fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium, but starting the fourth set with a poor service game allowed Zverev to reassert his authority and extinguish American dreams.Zverev did not initially know he had secured victory when Shelton hit a return long on championship point, only breaking out into a broad and slightly surprised smile after his team pointed out the score to him.Going into the 2026 season, few people would have backed Zverev to win two Grand Slam tournaments, with the German having already lost three major finals in a career which looked in danger of not living up to expectation.But injuries to his biggest rivals - Alcaraz missing the French Open and Wimbledon, with Sinner ruled out of the US Open - opened the door for Zverev.A below-par Zverev scraped through the opening rounds at Flushing Meadows in a series of early-morning finishes, but he gradually improved over a fortnight where he did not play a top-20 opponent until Shelton.Zverev had not lost to Shelton in their five previous meetings and immediately capitalised on a nervy start by his opponent.Shelton double-faulted on break point in the first game of the match, handing over the type of initiative that opponents often struggle to wrestle back from Zverev.Through the strength of his first serve, and his ability to unpick Shelton's weaker backhand in the baseline exchanges, Zverev rolled through the opening set and clinched it when Shelton hit another double fault on set point.Zverev continued to patiently draw mistakes from Shelton in the second set, but without being gifted a break when his only opportunity arrived in the fourth game.He instead showed why he has a strong tie-break record with another nerveless display and, unlike in the 2020 US Open final when he lost from a two-set lead, kept his composure in the pressure moments to secure a commanding victory.Addressing his team which is led by his father Alexander senior and brother Mischa, Zverev said: "We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now won two in the span of three months."I think God has seen how hard we have worked, how hard we have suffered and how much pain we went through."I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."Despite the bitter disappointment of losing Sunday's showpiece, Shelton will take pride from his run to a first major final, as well as further belief he can win a Grand Slam title.Shelton came into the tournament with confidence after winning the Canadian Open last month, but also with a point to prove after an underwhelming season at the Grand Slams.A chastening first-round exit at Wimbledon against Finnish qualifier Otto Virtanen was described by Shelton as "one of the toughest losses" of his career, acting as a wake-up call going into the North American hard court swing.He has bounced back superbly to come close to ending America's 23-year wait for somebody to finally follow in Roddick's footsteps.Shelton did not have an easy route to the final, needing to overcome a series of big-hitting opponents which included three former top-10 players as well as seven-time major champion Alcaraz.Shelton had never beaten a top-three opponent until powering past Alcaraz - who was playing in his first tournament for almost five months - in an epic quarter-final which ended at 3:34am.However, he could not double that tally against world number two Zverev.Shelton's recent success has been a product of developing his defensive skills and improving his weaker backhand, but not being able to execute his damaging forehand in crucial moments against Zverev proved costly.It was a reminder of the work the American number one still has to do at the highest level against the very best opponents."I'm excited with the progress that I feel that I've made, but this one stings 100%," said Shelton."I made too many errors when I had the ball there on my strings."

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Alexander Zverev beats Ben Shelton for second Grand Slam title

title: Swedish party blocs tied after Sunday vote, projections say
description: Early on Monday morning, Kristersson said it remained unclear who would form the next government."The voters have had their say, but we still don't ha
body: Early on Monday morning, Kristersson said it remained unclear who would form the next government."The voters have had their say, but we still don't have a final result. Which government will lead Sweden in the coming years is still an open question," he told supporters.No major media outlets have declared a winner yet.Sweden uses a mandate distribution voting system, a proportional representation method to elect "mandates", or "seats", in the Riksdag – the Swedish parliament. A party needs at least 4% of the vote to enter parliament.With 94% of votes reported, the left-wing bloc led by the Social Democrats was ahead with 176 mandates compared to the right-wing bloc's 173.Sweden has two major political blocs featuring four parties on the right and four on the left - meaning coalition and minority governments are relatively common.On Sunday night, Andersson - the leader of the country's main opposition party - urged supporters to wait for the final result, but added that if the current results hold, "Sweden will have a new government."Her party, the Social Democrats, have been a major force in Swedish politics since the end of World War Two.But SD - founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s - had been shunned for years until 2022 when it became the country's second largest party after campaigning on violent crime and immigration.Both Andersson's party and the far-right SD have lost support, according to early count results.As of Monday morning, the Social Democrats were on track for their worst result in more than a century with 28 per cent, while the count showed the far-right SD party was losing support for the first time since 2010 when it entered the Riksdag.Other parties comprising the left-wing bloc, including the Left Party, Greens and Centre Party have increased their support. Turnout also dropped to approximately 80%, down four points compared to the 2022 poll.After casting her vote on Sunday, Andersson laid out the choice facing the Swedish public: "Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats, something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of co-operation?"Kristersson, for his part, said it was important he and his alliance were able to continue their work."I think there is a genuine enthusiasm for us being able to continue our important work," he said after casting his ballot in his home municipality of Strangnas.National security, gang crime and welfare spending dominated the election campaign.

schema.headline: Swedish party blocs tied after Sunday vote, projections say

title: Buckingham Palace works uncover trove of everyday items dating back to 1800s
description: It revealed the monarch would work the room in a "clockwise direction", and that aides were asked to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with t
body: It revealed the monarch would work the room in a "clockwise direction", and that aides were asked to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the annual gathering."The British guests will be distributed throughout the State Rooms, except the Music Room and West Gallery, where they should be encouraged to talk to the Diplomats," the sheet reads.Blank Littlewoods Football Pool betting slips from 1957 and a scrap of West End theatre listings from The Standard newspaper in 1889 were also found, alongside fragments of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dated to around the mid-1800s. A pewter tankard, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards were included in the haul.Examples of electrical wire covered with vulcanised Indian rubber cabling were found. It was replaced as priority when the restoration began as it posed the greatest risk of fire to the building.Also discovered were pages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailing the "maximum security" prison where the Great Train Robbers were incarcerated.The article had pictures of Durham Prison, revealing that "the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings".Meanwhile, the whist drive ticket, priced at 6d or sixpence, would have taken place during the reign of King Charles III's grandfather, George VI, hosted by the Buckingham palace social club.

schema.headline: Buckingham Palace works uncover trove of everyday items dating back to 1800s

title: Danny Murphy column: 'Their intelligence and resilience was key' - how Man City earned 'statement win'
description: If you go to Old Trafford in a derby, go down to 10 men in the first 25 minutes and still come away with a 1-0 victory, it tells you a lot about your
body: If you go to Old Trafford in a derby, go down to 10 men in the first 25 minutes and still come away with a 1-0 victory, it tells you a lot about your players.Sunday's result was a statement win for Manchester City's new manager Enzo Maresca, who got his tactics spot on, but his team's performance will have showed him exactly what they are about.I am talking about the mentality, discipline, organisation and energy you need in order to get a result when things go wrong for you like that in a game.They were smart too, and that experience and ability not to panic goes a long way in football in situations like the one City faced following Phil Foden's early red card.City are used to always having most of the ball but they were fine without it against United. That is down to leadership and communication - not just from the manager, but from the players on the field.Maresca deserves plenty of credit for his decisions too, but he must be thinking he is a lucky man for having the group of players he does, because their intelligence and resilience was key.As I said on Match of the Day, if anyone is doubting the competitiveness of City this season, just watch that game.Figure caption, Haaland scores controversial winner as Manchester City win derby despite Foden red'City seemed to enjoy the challenge'When it was 11 v 11, I thought United were the better team.They pinned City back and were really bright going forward. Marcus Rashford, especially, was really positive and it felt like Michael Carrick's side were in the ascendancy.The sending-off, which was the right decision by the way, kind of stopped United's momentum a little bit and also basically told City how they were going to have to play - they were going to have to defend for most of the game.It is not what they are used to, but when you've got really experienced international players who are comfortable and calm, they don't really mind having to adapt.They actually seemed to enjoy the challenge, and straight away they were well-organised and very disciplined.United did not really create too much in the second part of the first half, other than a Rashford free-kick that hit the post, but I was thinking they would make a few tweaks at half-time and come out and really go after City. That didn't happen though.Image caption, After Foden was sent off after 23 minutes, Maresca made only one change in the first 80 minutes of the game, when he replaced Cherki with Ndiaye at half-time'It felt comfortable for City'United hit the post again in the second half, with Kobbie Mainoo's shot from distance, but they did not really create a clear-cut chance until Gianluigi Donnarumma saved from Bryan Mbeumo right at the end of the game.Other than that, their decision-making in the final third wasn't great. They were shooting from silly angles or, when they got in some good wide areas and put the ball in, there were not enough numbers in the box.United could also have changed their team around and brought on Benjamin Sesko earlier than they did, while I thought Rashford should have stayed on instead of Matheus Cunha because he was more of a threat.But whatever United did try, City managed the game brilliantly.Even at the time, I thought their winning goal really shouldn't have stood, because Enzo Fernandez impacts play and should have been ruled offside, but their defensive display was outstanding, and not just from their back four and central midfielders.Image caption, Carrick made two substitutions during Sunday's derby, replacing Youri Tielemans with Sesko after 67 minutes and then bringing on Joshua Zirkzee for Rashford after 83 minutes'Ndiaye gave City an extra dimension'City were also superb further up the field. Antoine Semenyo and Erling Haaland were keeping the ball when it was played up to them, as well as winning free-kicks or beating people.When he came on for Rayan Cherki, Iliman Ndiaye again did all of that brilliantly. He gave them a different dimension, and was a big reason they won the game.That substitution was a clever one by Maresca and brave too, because while Ndiaye is better than Cherki defensively, he is also a ball-carrier who travels with the ball better too.I remember Maresca making a couple of negative substitutions this time last year when his Chelsea side went down to 10 men early on at Old Trafford.They ended up losing the game and he got a bit of criticism for it, but this time he went with Ndiaye, and it worked a treat.He gave them an outlet and made some great runs - he was part of everything they did positively from an attacking point of view and was even involved in the goal - but also did his share of defending, and winning the ball back.As the game went on, it looked like United were the ones who looked tired despite having the extra man for so long.Maybe that was down to them playing on Thursday night, while City had their Champions League game on Tuesday, but it was not just energy that United were lacking.They simply did not have the know-how to cause City problems. Let's not forget Donnarumma's late save because it was a brilliant stop, but Maresca's men were comfortable most of the time.Danny Murphy was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.Figure caption, Refereeing decisions were 'baffling' - Rooney

schema.headline: Danny Murphy column: 'Their intelligence and resilience was key' - how Man City earned 'statement win'

title: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, Andy Burnham urges
description: The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting with some of the UK's biggest bosses.The prime minist
body: The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting with some of the UK's biggest bosses.The prime minister said those who take risks in business should be backed by government and local leaders should have the power to work with businesses.The current Labour government has been criticised for increasing costs for businesses, such as with the employer national insurance and minimum wage changes under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.Downing Street said Burnham will meet with the chief executives of BP, Shell, HSBC, Morrisons, Sainsbury's, BT, Vodafone, Rolls-Royce, and several others at Number 10.Ahead of the meeting, Burnham said he would give people "the confidence that if they have a great idea, they'll get all the support they need to bring it to life"."When local leaders have the tools to get things done and government works in partnership with business, you can pull in investment, create jobs and transform communities," he said.He added the government would be "a partner for growth to make every part of Britain better off".Burnham will host a reception for the business community where local leaders are invited before a private engagement with senior chief executives at Downing Street on Monday evening.The meeting comes as higher borrowing costs in the UK and other countries present problems for governments looking to spend money on business support or investment.Official data revealed a surprise boost in the economy in July partly driven by artificial intelligence (AI) investment, though experts expect growth to slow in the months ahead due to high energy prices.The US-Israel war with Iran has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices, affecting households and businesses.This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.The expectation of higher interest rates, as well as competition for debt from AI firms looking to spend money on development, has driven up the cost of government borrowing in many countries.However, many argue the UK has a particular problem with high government debt. The UK yield for 10-year bonds, a key measure of government debt costs, is higher than countries such as the US, France, and Japan.Experts say this is due to several factors affecting investor confidence in the UK, such as multiple prime ministers, chancellors and policy U-turns over a short period.In an interview with the BBC last week, Chancellor John Healey called for a restoration of "confidence about Britain" despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.Others have argued that the Labour government has created its own problems by increasing costs for businesses.Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "The way for the prime minister to get businesses thriving, delivering jobs and driving growth is to cut their taxes."Labour's jobs tax and employer red tape have been devastating for businesses. The consequence has been a drying-up of the jobs market, weaker investment and businesses facing ever greater costs."

schema.headline: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, Andy Burnham urges

title: The Pitt is up for 25 Emmys - but the show's biggest fans are real-life doctors
description: Image source, HBO MAXImage caption, The lead character Dr Michael Robinavitch, played by Noah Wyle, is a hardened and highly experienced emergency med
body: Image source, HBO MAXImage caption, The lead character Dr Michael Robinavitch, played by Noah Wyle, is a hardened and highly experienced emergency medicine consultantByHealth editorIt's a familiar sight: a crowded waiting room, trolleys in corridors, stressed doctors and nurses. But this isn't a typical A&E unit in the NHS, it's a Hollywood set with actors recreating the drama of an emergency department for TV series The Pitt.And among its biggest fans are real-life doctors."We finally feel validated for everything we go through every day," says Dr Tony Cirillo, President of the American College of Emergency Physicians.On Monday, The Pitt could become this year's most decorated series at the Emmys, America's most coveted TV honours, with 25 nominations.Doctors and others in the medical profession say, for them, it's the most realistic medical drama yet - which is why they love it.Image source, Warner BrothersImage caption, The show is a TV drama focusing on the staff of a fictional trauma centre in PittsburghImage source, Warner BrothersImage caption, Wyle (right) is a producer on the show as well as part of the writing teamThe series covers the life and work of the staff of Pittsburgh's Trauma Medical Centre, with each episode representing an hour of a day and there are 15 in each series.A constant thread through each episode is the noise, the pace of activity and the constant demands on the staff who never seem to get a break. Complex procedures and life-saving interventions are shown in graphic, and often, gory detail.The lead character Dr Michael Robinavitch, known as Dr Robby, is a hardened and highly experienced emergency medicine consultant (in US hospitals a senior emergency attending physician). Played by Noah Wyle, previously in the cast of mid-90s medical drama ER, he is an executive producer as well as part of the writing team, which includes qualified doctors.'The Pitt makes us feel validated'Wyle was invited to take part in a platform discussion at a prestigious conference with more than 6,000 emergency medicine experts in the audience."People came up to him and, as opposed to actors and athletes where they say they are amazing or love their work, people just said thank you to him," Cirillo says."The Pitt is more than just a good TV show – the term I use is validation."Social and ethical issues are often reflected. A stressed daughter who is caring for her sick mother leaves her in the emergency department and then can't be found.There are anguished conversations with parents who are desperate for their child to be kept alive, despite doctors saying there is no hope. Health inequalities are highlighted, with some patients struggling with the payments required in the US health system.Long waits and patient frustration are obvious shades of the NHS.And, based on our conversations, the series has become more popular in the UK with medics.Image source, Warner BrothersImage caption, Doctors say they like to see themselves represented on screen in shows like The PittDoctors seem ready to watch even in weeks when they have had punishing days or nights in A&E.One of them is Dr Fiona Hunter, vice president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine in Scotland."I wouldn't do it straight after a shift," she said. "We all need to decompress and debrief what we have experienced."But in between shifts, when I have got downtime, it's watchable, relatable. It makes me feel other people might get it."North Wales consultant Dr Rob Perry is another fan."I think it is reassuring when you see people portraying doctors and nurses in a similar job to your own and, though its not in the UK, they are doing their level best to give the best care they can," he said. 'A very common problem around the world'Doctors we spoke to do point out that each episode of The Pitt brings together several urgent trauma cases which typically might be spread across 24 hours or more.But Prof Damian Roland, a practising emergency medicine consultant, notes that the drama does illustrate wider health challenges.He thinks it puts the problems of the NHS in perspective."Virtually every emergency department in the world at the moment has not enough space to see patients," he says."It's a very common theme in The Pitt about the central character arguing with hospital management saying 'I need more flow, you can't just leave these patients here' – that's a very common problem.""In my work in the NHS, its very much we all work for one another and I like that we represent that on the show," says Sarah Tosh, a senior NHS nurse who is the series medical adviser."In The Pitt they've got a bit about the characters' day-to-day life, but it's more about their medicine, which patient they are doing and what they are going on to next."Image source, Warner BrothersImage caption, Gerran Howell (right) is a British actor nominated for an outstanding supporting actor award at the EmmysOne of the stars of The Pitt, Gerran Howell, was born and brought up in South Wales.With other actors he was put through a medical boot camp for speed learning of medical techniques and jargon. This included training on dummies and CPR practice.In a BBC Wales interview he was asked if he would like to train to be a doctor."I have such a newfound respect for the medical profession. It's maybe made me realise that I don't know how I would do this. I will stick to acting."Howell is nominated for an outstanding supporting actor award at the Emmys.The winners will be announced on 14 September at a ceremony in Los Angeles.The Pitt is available to stream on HBO Max in the UK and US.

schema.headline: The Pitt is up for 25 Emmys - but the show's biggest fans are real-life doctors

title: Meghan shares first glimpse of family life after return to UK
description: The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to  Instagram following their return to the UK. The 34-second clip, which
body: The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to  Instagram following their return to the UK. The 34-second clip, which features Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go, begins with Meghan, along with her husband Prince Harry, walking along a country path as she turns and says "come on, you". UK flag and heart emojis are shown throughout the video, which also shows their son Archie running towards deer as their daughter Lilibet rides her bike. Another clip sees Harry fishing with the children as their dog walks alongside the water. It's the first time the Duchess has posted her family on her Instagram grid since the Sussexes returned from the US after living in California. It is unclear when, or where, the footage posted on Sunday afternoon was taken, external, but one clip shows a pair of wellington boots walking on the spot in a puddle and the children also appear to be in waterproof boots as they head toward the deer.   The UK has had a wet start to September after experiencing its hottest summer on record.The post offers a rare glimpse into the lives of seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet. Whereas Meghan does occasionally show the couple's children on social media, their faces are often obscured as they are photographed from behind or their faces are hidden by their parents.  Alongside all the outside footage, there is also a moment showing a child's feet in front of an open fire. Last month, a spokesman for the Sussexes would not confirm the family's arrival in the UK, but did say they were bringing their dogs, Mia and Pula, with them. The couple adopted a black Labrador retriever several years ago, which is seen several times in the clip. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020. They have not returned to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals. It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area, and Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in a school. Last week, a spokesperson for both the Duke and Duchess said the couple were surprised by a letter send by the Prince's father, King Charles III, clarifying they would remain non-working royals. The spokesperson said the couple "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".The letter, sent on behalf of the King, spelt out the non-working royal status of Prince Harry and Meghan.They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.

schema.headline: Meghan shares first glimpse of family life after return to UK

title: Nepal floods: The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'
description: The Himalayas are approaching a dangerous threshold as glaciers melt faster, glacial lakes grow more unstable and the mountains face a widening gap in
body: The Himalayas are approaching a dangerous threshold as glaciers melt faster, glacial lakes grow more unstable and the mountains face a widening gap in monitoring, according to new research.The findings come in the aftermath of devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, which killed more than 1,300 people and caused widespread destruction, highlighting the growing risks from a rapidly changing Himalayan environment.Himalayan glaciers are now losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, the report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with the Integrated Mountain Initiative and with technical contributions from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, says.Yet only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region are being monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, according to the report.That monitoring gap matters because the physical landscape is changing rapidly.As glaciers retreat, they can leave behind expanding lakes held back by unstable deposits of rock and ice. At the same time, warming is destabilising permafrost - permanently frozen ground that can thaw as temperatures rise - and high mountain slopes, increasing the possibility of cascading hazards, the report says.India already has evidence of the scale of the risk. Some 18% of Indian land is Himalayan, yet the region accounts for about 35% of disasters, according to the report.The government told parliament in July that 56 glacial lakes had been classified as "very high risk", external following a 2025 scientific assessment of 189 high-risk lakes in the Indian Himalayan region. The Central Water Commission is monitoring 2,485 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares across India's Himalayan river basins, the government said.The Himalayas have already seen devastating examples of what can happen when glacial lakes burst their natural dams. In 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim killed at least 70 people and caused widespread damage to roads, bridges and hydropower projects. In 2021, a similar disaster in Uttarakhand killed more than 200 people after a massive flood swept through the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys. But the danger is not confined to spectacular floods.The Himalayas are a vast natural water system feeding rivers that sustain hundreds of millions of people across South Asia. ICIMOD says "peak water", external is expected around mid-century in most Hindu Kush Himalayan river basins - the point at which glacier runoff reaches its maximum before declining as glaciers lose mass.The new research puts an unusually large economic number on that dependency. It estimates that Himalayan water underpins roughly 20% of India's GDP, sustaining wheat, rice, tea, hydropower and pilgrimage economies. Yet the mountain states capture only about 5% of that value, it says."The Himalayas are the Third Pole," said economist Lord Nicholas Stern, chair of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics. "Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it.""This is national and international infrastructure," he said, warning that the ecological system underpinning it is "approaching a tipping point".Not all the forces driving glacier loss are beyond the region's control.The Systemiq research estimates that roughly a third of Himalayan glacier melt is driven by black carbon, much of it originating from brick kilns in the plains. Soot deposited on snow and ice absorbs more sunlight and accelerates melting.Unlike global greenhouse-gas emissions, black-carbon pollution is a lever that India and its neighbours can act on directly, the report argues."The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point, with millions of lives and livelihoods hanging in the balance," said Arushi Chopra, Systemiq's senior director and lead author. "Glaciers are melting faster than they were a decade ago."The report proposes 10 priority transitions, ranging from reducing black-carbon emissions and expanding glacier monitoring to improving disaster early-warning systems and changing the way tourism is developed in the mountains.One priority is to strengthen disaster preparedness, with governments agreeing in advance what action to take when hazards emerge - from evacuation to protecting vulnerable infrastructure.Another is to rethink tourism. The Indian Himalayan region receives roughly 400 million tourist visits a year, according to the report, and researchers argue that the objective should shift from maximising visitor numbers towards generating value that is retained and reinvested locally.Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said the risks were becoming increasingly complex."Glaciers are retreating, permafrost and high-mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable, and communities and infrastructure downstream face growing risks from complex and cascading hazards," he said.And those risks do not stop at the borders drawn across the Himalayas. Such hazards, Gyamtsho said, "do not respect national borders, and no single country can address them alone".That makes cross-border monitoring, shared risk information and early-warning systems, and joint investment in resilience increasingly urgent - not just to save lives, but to protect the livelihoods and economies of hundreds of millions of people who depend on the mountains.

schema.headline: Nepal floods: The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'

title: September reset: Why now is the time to start a new routine and how to stick to it
description: Why I'm doing a September reset and how you can create a new routineImage source, Cami SophiaImage caption, Cami Sophia sees September as a chance to
body: Why I'm doing a September reset and how you can create a new routineImage source, Cami SophiaImage caption, Cami Sophia sees September as a chance to get ahead with her goalsByEmily HoltThe lazy hazy days of summer may feel like a distant memory as September shifts our energy back to business and forward to new adventures.It's the month when many of us embark on a new chapter, whether it's university, college or a new job or simply getting back to work and the school run.It's also the time that "September Reset" trends on social media - the kind, chill sister of New Year's Resolutions. Instead of strict rules and major life overhauls, creators are sharing small changes aimed at finishing the year strong."It's getting ahead of the game," says Cami Sophia, 24, who has shared her new rituals on TikTok. Here's why September could be the right time for a reset and how to create a new routine that lasts.What's Up Docs? Should you get back into a routine?  Listen now. For Cami, a content creator and podcast host from Northampton, September spells the end of summer spontaneity and a time to restore order."If you've been away for the summer you've probably not had a massive routine," she says. "And if you're a parent, then you've got kids at home and it's just a bit more chaotic," she says.September feels like "back to school...getting back into your own rhythm", she adds.It is the perfect time to "get everything sorted", she says "So when you get to January you're not trying to do everything at once.For Bas Verplanken, professor emeritus of social psychology at the University of Bath, September is a chance to "reorient yourself".He says his research suggests people who experienced a big change such as moving house "were more responsive to an intervention aimed at promoting sustainable behaviours" than comparable people who had not moved house."It's really an exciting way of looking at disruption," he told Chris and Xand van Tulleken on their What's Up Docs? podcast.If your daily commute or school run works for you then relax back into them."But if there are alternative ways of doing things, explore it, this is the time to do it, and to make those changes," says Verplanken.What will you reset?Image source, Cami SophiaImage caption, Cami preps meals and books workout classes in advance to stick to her routineTikTok is awash with videos on how to "lock in" starting small - declutter your room, clear out your wardrobe, go for a walk, start a new book.But Cami warns against videos showing spreadsheets of radical changes."It's very easy to look at all of these things and what you should apparently be doing and get really overwhelmed," she says.Cami starts her own reset by "looking at the goals I set at the start of the year and see what I actually still want to do - and then what I need to do to get from A to B".Then she recommends picking three small "non-negotiables"."They could be to have fruit with your breakfast, have veg with dinner and have a glass of water before you drink coffee," she says.She advises small changes that require little effort - she is getting back into sleep patterns by setting alarms.The secret to sticking to itCami says planning is key - something she does on a Sunday morning. "I go, okay, these are my meals for the week. These are my workouts for the week. Even plan your outfits for the work day if you really want to because it saves you time," she says.Then she takes steps to "limit the choices" she has to stray from her routine."I will meal prep three days worth of overnight oats. Naturally, I'm going to grab those in the morning because they are made and ready. I've removed the friction of grabbing a quick meal or not having any breakfast."Verplanken agrees the secret to making new habits that last is setting yourself up so that your new behaviours are the easiest option for reaching your goal.He advises designing a routine where your habits can become "effortless"."They are specific plans of where, when, and what you will do," he says."Let's say, losing weight, you can think when I go to the supermarket, I'm going to look specifically each time [at] the fat and sugar content [of food]. It's a very specific plan."This means making the right choices when are facing the food shelf happen automatically "because you have already planned the situation in which you have to act".If this is done frequently, Verplanken says it becomes "extremely effective" to turn these habits into your routine.

schema.headline: September reset: Why now is the time to start a new routine and how to stick to it

title: First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to meet in Cardiff
description: The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss ways of "working more closely", including on con
body: The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss ways of "working more closely", including on constitutional issues.It will be the first face-to-face meeting between the three nationalist leaders since Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth took office in May.Ap Iorwerth will host the SNP's leader John Swinney and Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill on Monday morning. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald will also attend.He will hold further talks with Swinney in the afternoon with both men expected to sign an agreement on "future collaboration in areas of shared interest".For the first time since devolution began Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.A Plaid spokesperson said ap Iorwerth's meeting with Swinney, O'Neill and McDonald was "an opportunity for the leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Féin to come together and talk about how we can work more closely on the issues that matter to people across our nations"."Following the historic Senedd election in Wales and the changing political landscape across these islands, there is a strong case for practical political cooperation on areas including energy, the economy and our relationship with Europe, as well as on the wider political and constitutional questions facing our nations and on the right to self-determination," they added.Swinney believed their was "undeniable" momentum behind constitutional change."Every nation across these islands is standing at a moment of incredible constitutional opportunity," he said."There is a growing consensus that the Westminster system simply is not fit for purpose and does not work for ordinary people. "Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accepted that himself - and the people of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have made it clear at the ballot box."The meetings come days after the matter of Scottish independence resurfaced in the Commons.During Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham appeared to indicate a second referendum could be held in Scotland if there was clear public support for a vote. He compared the situation to the conditions for a border poll in Northern Ireland explaining the Good Friday Agreement made clear a border poll would be "considered by the Northern Ireland Secretary when there is a clear consensus in the country, when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered"."I would say that it is exactly the same situation in Scotland," he added.The apparent softening in tone was welcomed by Swinney before Burnham clarified that another Scottish referendum remained "off limits". A referendum on Scottish independence in September 2014 saw the country vote to remain part of the UK by a margin of 55% to 45%.Ap Iorwerth was appointed the first non-Labour first minister of Wales after May's Senedd election.Whilst he has ruled out pushing for a referendum on Welsh independence during his party's first term in government, he has said he wants to lead a "national conversation" about the issue.His government intends to set up a national commission to "lay the foundations" for future plans for Welsh independence.In the meantime, Welsh ministers are also asking for extra powers to be transferred to Wales, including over policing and youth justice.Burnham has said he is "open" to the idea. In Northern Ireland, the first and deputy first minister have identical powers and responsibilities and the DUP's Emma Little-Pengelly is the deputy first minister.Little-Pengelly of unionist party the DUP criticised O'Neill for attending. Monday's talks are likely to cover the way the devolved nations are funded by the UK government.Welsh ministers have long called for the Barnett funding formula to be reformed, claiming it disadvantages Wales.However, it is argued Scotland does well from the formula.Before he became prime minister Burnham made the case for change, but on his recent visit to Wales he played down the prospect of reform.The devolved leaders will meet the prime minister next month. The UK government said: "The prime minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the union."Welsh Conservatives leader Darren Millar said: "Instead of obsessing about independence, the first minister should be focused on dealing with the crisis engulfing the Welsh NHS and the declining standards in Welsh schools."Reform UK Wales said: "Plaid Cymru is showing its true colours by meeting with Sinn Féin and the Scottish separatists."

schema.headline: First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to meet in Cardiff

title: Referees body admits error of judgement over Erling Haaland derby winner
description: The Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref has admitted an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's Manchester City winner against Manchester
body: The Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref has admitted an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's Manchester City winner against Manchester United.As City celebrated a remarkable derby victory over Manchester United, there were questions as to whether Haaland's winning goal should have stood in a match fraught with controversy.The striker scored in the 60th minute at Old Trafford, turning home at the back post from Josko Gvardiol's cross before it was disallowed on the field for offside.Following intervention from the video assistant referee, the goal was awarded - the Norwegian ruled to have been played onside by Patrick Dorgu's boot.But there was debate as to whether the offside Enzo Fernandez, diving at the ball in a more central position than Haaland, was interfering with play.In a statement, Pro Ref said: "It was established that Enzo Fernandez did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective."However, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review."Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place."United defender Lisandro Martinez said it was an "injustice" while boss Michael Carrick said he was "confused" by the decision.The goal came after City had gone down to 10 men in the first half when Phil Foden was shown a straight red card for kicking out at United captain Bruno Fernandes.Foden was dismissed by referee Michael Oliver on 23 minutes after kicking the midriff of Fernandes while he was on the turf.When Haaland's goal was ruled out as offside on the field, few questioned the decision as the City striker looked to have drifted beyond United's defensive line.The lines drawn by the VAR showed Haaland to be onside thanks to Dorgu's boot. But it was the positioning and involvement of Fernandez that left many pundits astounded and unsure if it was a legitimate goal.Gvardiol's cross took a slight deflection off the boot of Dorgu before finding its way to Haaland at the back post, while Fernandez was clearly attempting a diving header in the middle of the six-yard box but he did not touch the ball.Fernandez appeared to be in an offside position, ahead of Dorgu's boot, but VAR deemed it to be a legitimate goal as he did not touch the ball while United defender Martinez was also closing in.The Premier League Match Centre said on X: "VAR checked the referee's call of no goal for offside - and determined that Haaland was in an onside position and recommended that the goal was awarded."The VAR also deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn't play the ball."Dale Johnson, BBC Sport football issues correspondentThe curiosity about this incident is that the goal was initially disallowed for the wrong reason. Haaland was flagged offside when he shouldn't have been.But as it turned out, the goal should have been ruled out because Fernandez was offside.There is one key part of the offside law which applies to Fernandez here. A player is offside if they are:"Clearly attempting to play a ball which is close when this action impacts on an opponent."Both parts of that clause must be met. It is possible for a player in an offside position to attempt to play a ball and not commit an offence – there must be impact on an opponent too.As the ball came in, Fernandez threw himself to try to head it, with Martinez directly behind him.Video assistant referee Matt Donohue should ask himself if Fernandez's action would have influenced Martinez.In other words: If Fernandez had not jumped for the attempted header, would Martinez have made a different decision over playing the ball?If the ball had been out of reach for Fernandez, or for Martinez, then there is an argument to give the goal.And also: There would have been no offside had Fernandez made no attempt to play the ball.But he did. And as it went just a yard in front of Martinez too, it is very difficult to argue Fernandez did not commit an offside offence.There is also an argument that the actions of Fernandez influence the positioning of goalkeeper Senne Lammens.However, the goal was originally ruled out for offside against Haaland - which was incorrect. So that decision had to be overturned. And then, the VAR should have sent referee Michael Oliver to the monitor for the subjective offence by Fernandez.It would have created the odd situation where a disallowed goal was reviewed to remain ruled out - but this is what should have happened.It was a clear offside offence by Fernandez and will go down as a VAR mistake.Was the VAR too concerned with a possible touch by Fernandez?If so, did the VAR forget that Fernandez was offside, and not consider the subjective offence? It seems to be the most logical explanation.A similar thing happened in a game between Arsenal and Brentford in February 2023 when a goal by an offside Christian Norgaard was not disallowed.With Haaland's goal settling the match, United were unsurprisingly disappointed by the decision."I think it was offside," said Martinez. "And what I can't understand is the rules. I want to be calm now, I want to control myself. "It's so hard because you lose a derby, you lose three points at home, and every season they're [referees] coming to our club, they explain for one hour the rules, and they look so confident with that, and then after [there are] five or six people doing these kind of mistakes in the Premier League - it's unacceptable."It's the best league in the world, you have the best teams in the world, the best players in the world, and now we have to go home with this injustice."United boss Carrick also expressed his confusion."We put things in place in the game now, we have people in offices with all the screens for this decision," he said. "It's more worrying about if that's the interpretation of football now. If that's the interpretation of not interfering in the game now, that's really worrying for me. It's a staggering explanation."The decision isn't going to change the season, but it's had a major impact on the game."Wayne Rooney, part of the BBC's MOTD team, said: "Surely it's offside. Martinez is impacted by Fernandez's movement, and he is offside."I am so sick of VAR. It is horrendous, it takes all the emotion out of the game and to not see it… anyone who has played the game recognises he is offside. To get it so wrong is baffling."Former Tottenham midfielder Danny Murphy, added: "If Enzo doesn't make the run Martinez sticks wth Haaland, The second person it effects is the goalkeeper. It makes it so simple and obvious and somehow they have missed the impact Enzo Fernandez has on the players around him."Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I think we'll see some sort of apology from the referee's association, there's no doubt Fernandez is playing that ball and is trying to put off Martinez. I think it's one they'll recognising they got wrong."Micah Richards added: "I think it's been a bad day for referees. They got the Foden decision wrong and the Fernandez decision wrong. I think they got it so wrong but I don't think it takes anything away from City's performance."Meanwhile, City boss Maresca said: "I think it was onside clearly so it's good."The goal came after a first half laced with controversy, with Foden shown a straight red for kicking out at midfielder Fernandes.City midfielder Foden picked up the ball wide on the right-hand side in his own half and was closed down by Fernandes, who tripped him.Foden then kicked out at the body of the Portuguese midfielder while on the ground and was shown a straight red card by the referee.Replays showed that Fernandes kicked Foden in the back first, before the England international retaliated.The incident was checked by the VAR, who confirmed the on-field decision; Fernandes was not shown a card.Pundits were divided on whether Foden should have seen red and whether Fernandes was the man at fault.Former Manchester United forward Rooney did not believe it was a red, saying "it was more of a flick or a gesture, than a kick out".Neville said he was "surprised" Fernandes did not receive a booking for his role while Roy Keane said the fault lay with the Portuguese midfielder."Foden gets up and reacts obviously, so he's sent off," he said. "Fernandes catches him and gives him a little kick. I guess it's classed as violent. But Fernandes is the one who is violent here, I don't think Foden should have a red card."Dale Johnson, BBC Sport's issues correspondent, said: "The referee and VAR would have to deem it violent conduct rather than just petulance from Fernandes."The guidance changed some years ago to factor that in, so David Beckham's kick on Diego Simeone in the 1998 World Cup would not result in a sending off today."It looked to me like there was little to no contact from Fernandes, and if there was it was limited force and wasn't followed through."So Bruno's act would be seen as a yellow card offence, which the VAR obviously can't get involved in."

schema.headline: Referees body admits error of judgement over Erling Haaland derby winner

title: Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
description: US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts."You have a lot of very neg
body: US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts."You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC that staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.Coxon – who has also worked at OpenAI  – welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.On one hand, the sector is seen as a huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.In August, OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.The ChatGPT-maker said it was adding new measures after its AI agents bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.The Trump administration argues that the US must maintain global tech dominance as a matter of national security, though it has admitted a need for vigilance around the risks posed by the emerging technology. The weekend call by major AI executives sparked discussion in Washington, where lawmakers are facing pressure to address those potential risks around rapid AI developments. On Sunday, Speaker Mike Johnson, the top House Republican, urged caution about rushing AI regulation during an appearance on CNN's Jake Tapper on State of the Union,  arguing it could "smother American innovation"."If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American," he said. "So, we've got to have balance. We've got to have steady hands at the wheel."Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries argued for "decisive action" by lawmakers.He told George Stephanopoulos on ABC's This Week that the US should slow down "the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely".Responding to recent comments from the AI industry, tech investor David Sacks, who serves on Trump's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, called on the companies to police themselves. "Stop pretending you need anyone else's permission," he posted on X."So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it... Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it."Still, there is at least some cross-party consensus on AI regulation. In July, a group of House Democrats and Republicans introduced the Frontier Act, a bipartisan bill that seeks to establish a national safety and oversight framework for AI."Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway," Rep Lori Trahan, a Massachusetts Democrat who co-authored the bill, wrote on X this week. "It's past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job."

schema.headline: Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down

title: Spanish Grand Prix: How VSC cost Lando Norris race win - and should F1 change the rules?
description: Lando Norris says he was "insanely unlucky" to lose what seemed like a certain win in the Spanish Grand Prix because of the timing of a virtual safety
body: Lando Norris says he was "insanely unlucky" to lose what seemed like a certain win in the Spanish Grand Prix because of the timing of a virtual safety car.McLaren's Norris was leading comfortably when the VSC was called, seconds after he had passed the pit lane entry.That allowed Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen to pit under the VSC, saving time, while the caution period ended before Norris could make it around to the pits again.Of the VSC, Norris said: "It is a rule that should not define a whole race.""I was the only one on the whole grid that didn't get the chance to do the pit stop," he said. "That's just unfortunate."There's been plenty of times where I've gained from it in the past and times where I've lost from it, and it's racing, but never when fighting for a win."So, it's probably one of the first times a win has been lost simply because of it."After taking pole position with a lap his team principal Andrea Stella described as "a masterpiece", Norris was leading Antonelli by more than six seconds after 13 laps in Madrid.He had just passed the pit entry at the end of lap 14 when a VSC was called because Lance Stroll's Aston Martin had stopped in the run-off area at Turn 20, while  Antonelli and Verstappen were far enough behind to pit.The VSC, which controls all cars to a specified maximum speed, then ended shortly before Norris completed the next lap, at the end of which he pitted.Because a stop under the VSC costs 11 seconds less race time than one under green-flag conditions, Norris lost sufficient time that Antonelli and Verstappen were able to pass him.Norris lost a further five seconds because of problems with his two right-hand side tyres at the stop and emerged from the pits more than 15 seconds behind Antonelli and more than nine adrift of Verstappen.He caught the Red Bull before the end of the race but as overtaking was virtually impossible on the new Madring street circuit, he was stuck in third place.Race-winner Antonelli, who extended his championship lead to 81 points, acknowledged Norris' bad fortune. "If I have to be realistic and honest, today we didn't deserve to win," he said. "Lando deserved to win, and so I think our result was probably P2 or even P3."The short duration of the VSC in this case was exactly why Norris was railing against the situation.Every other driver in the field had the opportunity to decide whether to pit or not - the only driver not given that option was Norris.The pit lane entry is before the final corner at the Madring, and Norris was in the last corner when it was called.The VSC ended when Norris was in Turn 21, the corner before the pit entry, on lap 15. Antonelli, having stopped, was behind him in Turn 19.On most circuits, Norris would have had a chance to pass Verstappen and perhaps even do the same to Antonelli before the end, given his pace advantage on the day, but as Antonelli put it: "In the race, you're just stuck behind."Norris was withering in his criticism of the track layout, saying: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes, 'Mint.'" But he did say there was "a lot of opportunity" to improve it for next year.After the race, one question asked of McLaren was whether pitting on the following lap was the best idea, or should Norris have stayed out?Norris said: "I had to come in at the end of the lap because it was the only chance."It was still effectively some pit loss, (but) the fact that everyone's kind of on colder tyres and you're still minimising the pit loss."The medium tyre (on which Norris had started the race) was destroyed and the hard tyre (to which Antonelli and Verstappen switched) was amazing."But the pace was very, very strong and on the hard tyre... I know they were stuck (behind Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who stayed out under the VSC), we caught up 13, 14 seconds or more, almost. So, plenty of positives. A day full of positives, just one thing let it all down."McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "We considered staying out, but you have to accept the fact that now you are on relatively used medium tyres. And the people behind you will be on new hard. So you're never going to open a gap on people on new hard."The other question was whether McLaren would have been wise to anticipate that the race director would call the VSC and pit Norris before it was deployed.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "In hindsight, that would have been a good idea."But he pointed out that, in the moment, it would have come with risks. The long pit lane at the Madring - the longest on the calendar - meant a pit stop cost a lot of time.Stella said: "I would have to review with my engineers, see whether it was kind of obvious that it would end up in a virtual safety car. Therefore, you try to anticipate or not."Here, the problem is that you need to be extremely careful, because it's 27 seconds if you don't pit under a virtual safety car."So if you get it wrong, it would be extremely penalising. From the lead, you pit unnecessarily, and now you have lost the victory."So a good rule is to respond to what is a fact, to what is the real condition of the circuit."But we will definitely take a look as to whether in these conditions it was just simply, you know, obvious that he would end up in a virtual safety car. I cannot answer at the moment."After the race, Norris and Verstappen said this kind of scenario had been discussed by drivers many times with governing body the FIA."I think there's always probably some cons to doing it, but it's tough," Norris said."I've won from it in the past, I've lost from it in the past. Over the course of a season, it's hard to know if it's a good thing or a bad thing."It probably equals out over time. Of course, it just hurts more, the fact that I lose a win. You know, there's literally nothing I could do as a driver today to do a better job."Verstappen said: "We'll probably talk about it in the next briefing and see if there is anything that can be done."Stella added: "Perhaps there's a wider reflection that the Formula 1 community should apply as to whether you keep things like they are or you introduce ways of maintaining more fairness."Offering the personal opinion. I'm puzzled myself as to what's right."Is it correct to give enough duration such that everyone will have been subject to the same track conditions? So, for instance, the virtual safety car lasts at least one full lap? Or you just keep it in the hands of the gods, and sometimes you are lucky, sometimes you are not. I'm not sure myself."But in general, there's the right place to have this sort of conversation, which is the Strategy Advisory Committee (SAC). And this is a topic that may be added to the agenda and discussed over there."But if there is to be a change, it will have to be a change that goes through the SAC, then the F1 Commission, and then we'll have to go at some stage to the sporting regulations."But I would envisage that this is a relatively lengthy process, unless there's a big push from F1, from the institutions, FIA or F1, to say, like, 'we need to make this different'."
